title: Touching the earth
hook: Mara asks who witnesses his right to that seat; he touches the ground, and the earth answers

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mara: the tempter whose storms and weapons fell as flowers. The arrows become flowers.

Have you ever been asked, out loud, what gives you the right? What makes you think you can do this job, hold this opinion, take up this space? It's one of the oldest weapons there is. It doesn't hurt the body. It goes straight for whether you belong. Mara's army has failed; the rocks and arrows have fallen as flowers. So Mara stops attacking and starts arguing. This seat, he says, belongs to me. Who are you to sit there? His whole army roars behind him: we are his witnesses! Now, who is yours?
screen: `WHAT GIVES YOU THE RIGHT?` → `THIS SEAT BELONGS TO ME.` → `WHO IS YOUR WITNESS?`

segments.voice: It's a lonely question. Mara has a whole army to speak for him. The wanderer is alone under a tree at night. In the telling, he answers that no living being is present to be his witness. But across countless lives, he says, he has given and given, practicing generosity and patience again and again. Then he moves his right hand. He draws it out from his lap, lets it rest over his right knee, and touches the ground with his fingertips. The earth itself will speak for him. And the earth answers, the telling says, with a roar like thunder: I am his witness. Mara's elephant kneels. The army scatters. Southeast Asia adds a beloved scene: the earth appears as a goddess, wrings out her long hair, and from it pours all the water of his past good deeds, a flood that sweeps Mara's army away. You'll see her in temples in Thailand, Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar. And the gesture is everywhere. Check the right hand on almost any seated Buddha statue. If it's reaching down to touch the ground, that's this moment: the earth-touching gesture, maybe the most common pose in all of Buddhist art. When someone asks what gives you the right, you don't have to shout louder. You can put your hand on the ground. The earth under you, and the good you've actually done, is witness enough.
screen: `NO ONE HERE TO SPEAK FOR HIM.` · `HIS HAND REACHES TO THE GROUND.` · `THE EARTH ROARS: I AM HIS WITNESS.` · `THE MOST COMMON POSE IN ART.` · then, large: `THE EARTH IS YOUR WITNESS.`

segments.voice: Reach down and touch the ground with your right hand: the floor, the grass, the carpet, or, if you can't reach, press your feet firmly into the floor. Feel it, solid, holding you up, asking nothing, and bring to mind one good thing you have actually done; small is fine, a kindness, an honest word, a promise kept. Let the ground and that memory be your witnesses; right now, you don't need anyone else to vouch for you.
Bhūmisparśa. The earth-touching gesture: the wanderer's right hand reaching down to call the earth as his witness, now carved on countless Buddha statues.
Your line: the earth is your witness. The hand on the ground says it without a word. That's day fifty-three.

howItsDone: The earth-touching gesture (bhumisparsha mudra) is one of the most common poses in Buddhist statues, and in Southeast Asia many temples honor the earth goddess who wrings the waters of merit from her hair.

original.note: Sanskrit: earth-touching, as in bhūmisparśa mudrā, the earth-witness gesture.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha statue is just resting its hand on its knee.
what it means: the hand reaches down to call the earth as witness to his right to the seat of awakening.

what a scholar hears: the Nidanakatha has the earth roar in witness to his past generosity (as Vessantara); the earth goddess (Thai Mae Thorani) wringing her hair is a later Southeast Asian development.

sources.ref: Nidanakatha (introduction to the Jataka): Mara's claim and the earth as witness
